# What To Ask For

> Backend building blocks for AI-built apps. Describe a need in plain words, get the name of the piece, when you need it, 2 to 3 ways to build it, and a copy-paste prompt with acceptance checks.

Agents: fetch /entries.json for everything in one file (search the needs, aliases and keywords fields), or /api/<id>.json for one entry. Each entry page is plain HTML at /e/<id>/index.html.

Each entry in entries.json has a category field. Categories: background (Background work and scheduling), payments (Payments and billing), auth (Auth and accounts), email (Email and notifications), files (Files and uploads), data (Data and databases), api (APIs and integrations), security (Security and abuse), deploys (Deploys, uptime and monitoring), ai (AI features), performance (Performance and caching), search (Search), features (Common app features), privacy (Analytics and privacy).

## Entries

### Background work and scheduling

- [Scheduled job](e/scheduled-jobs/index.html): Code that runs on a clock instead of when someone clicks. A scheduler wakes up, checks what is due and runs it. JSON: api/scheduled-jobs.json
- [Background job queue](e/background-job-queue/index.html): The web request saves a job and answers right away. A separate worker picks up the job, does the slow part and stores the result. The page checks back for it. JSON: api/background-job-queue.json
- [Retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue](e/retries-and-dead-letter-queue/index.html): When a call to another service fails, try again after a wait that grows each time, with a little randomness so clients don't all retry at once. After a set number of attempts, park the job in a dead-letter queue or a failed state where a person can see it and replay it. JSON: api/retries-and-dead-letter-queue.json
- [Time zone handling](e/time-zones/index.html): Store moments in time as UTC, store each user's time zone as an IANA name like America/New_York, and convert only when you show a time or schedule one. An offset like -05:00 is not a time zone, because it changes with daylight saving. JSON: api/time-zones.json
- [Transactional outbox](e/outbox-pattern/index.html): Instead of saving a record and then sending a message (two steps that can half fail), you save the record and an outbox row in one database transaction. A separate worker reads the outbox and sends the messages, retrying until each one is done. JSON: api/outbox-pattern.json
- [Job status and progress UI](e/job-progress-ui/index.html): A record for each long job (queued, running, percent, done or failed, result link) plus a screen that reads it. The page asks for updates every few seconds or listens for them, survives a refresh, and shows a real error when the job fails. JSON: api/job-progress-ui.json

### Payments and billing

- [Webhook signature verification](e/webhook-signature-verification/index.html): A webhook is another service calling your URL when something happens. The sender signs each request with a shared secret. Your server recomputes the signature from the raw body and rejects anything that doesn't match or is too old. JSON: api/webhook-signature-verification.json
- [Idempotent webhook handling](e/idempotent-webhooks/index.html): Providers retry webhooks and sometimes deliver the same event more than once or out of order. Idempotent handling means running the same event twice has the same result as running it once. The usual way: save the event id first and skip it if it's already done. JSON: api/idempotent-webhooks.json
- [Subscription billing](e/subscription-billing/index.html): A recurring charge tied to a plan. The payment provider runs the billing schedule. Your app keeps a copy of each customer's subscription status, updated from webhooks, and grants features from that status. Changing plans mid-period creates a proration: a credit for unused time on the old plan and a charge for the new one. JSON: api/subscription-billing.json
- [Failed payment recovery (dunning)](e/failed-payment-recovery/index.html): Renewal charges fail all the time: expired cards, low balances, bank blocks. Dunning is what happens next: retry the charge on a schedule, email the customer a link to update their card, show a banner in the app, and decide when access ends if it never gets paid. JSON: api/failed-payment-recovery.json
- [Usage-based billing](e/usage-based-billing/index.html): Charging for how much someone used instead of a flat fee. Your app records each billable event in its own database first, then reports totals to the billing system, which adds them to the invoice. Prepaid credits are the other common shape: the user buys a balance and each use draws it down. JSON: api/usage-based-billing.json
- [Free trial (with or without a card)](e/free-trials/index.html): A period of paid features before the first charge. Asking for a card up front means fewer people start, but more of them end up paying. Without a card more people try it, and you must decide what happens at the end: cancel, pause, or ask for a card. JSON: api/free-trials.json
- [Per-seat team billing](e/seat-billing/index.html): A team subscription whose quantity equals the number of paid members. Adding or removing a member changes the quantity, the payment provider prorates the difference, and your app blocks invites past the paid count if you want hard limits. JSON: api/seat-billing.json
- [Plan limits and entitlements](e/plan-limits/index.html): One place in your code that answers "is this account allowed to do this, and how much is left?" based on its plan. Every feature asks it instead of checking plan names itself, and limit checks happen in the same transaction as the work they guard. JSON: api/plan-limits.json
- [Refunds and chargebacks](e/refunds-disputes/index.html): The flow for giving money back, and for answering when a customer's bank pulls it back for you. Your app listens for refund and dispute events, updates access, and keeps the records you need to respond to a dispute before the deadline. JSON: api/refunds-disputes.json

### Auth and accounts

- [Password reset tokens](e/password-reset/index.html): A one-time, short-lived link emailed to the account owner that lets them set a new password. The token is random and stored only as a hash (or signed), and it stops working after use, after it expires, and once the password changes. JSON: api/password-reset.json
- [Magic link sign-in](e/magic-links/index.html): The user types their email and gets a link that signs them in. The link holds a random one-time token that expires in minutes. Email security scanners often open links before the person does, so a safe design shows a confirm button and only signs in on that click. JSON: api/magic-links.json
- [Social login (OAuth and OpenID Connect)](e/social-login/index.html): Users sign in with an account they already have. Your app sends them to the provider, gets back a code, and swaps it on the server for tokens that say who they are. Use a library for this, keep the requested permissions small, and only link to an existing account when the provider says the email is verified. JSON: api/social-login.json
- [Sessions vs JWT](e/sessions-vs-jwt/index.html): Two ways to remember who is logged in. A session is a random id in a cookie that points to data on your server, so you can end it any time. A JWT is a signed token that carries the user's details itself, so the server doesn't look anything up, but it stays valid until it expires unless you add a revocation list. JSON: api/sessions-vs-jwt.json
- [Roles and permissions](e/roles-and-permissions/index.html): Rules for who may do what. Users get a role (owner, admin, member, viewer) and each action checks the role on the server. Hiding a button only changes what people see. The server must refuse the request too. JSON: api/roles-and-permissions.json
- [Multi-tenant data isolation](e/multi-tenant-isolation/index.html): Keeping each customer's data separate when they all share one app and one database. Every row carries a tenant id, every query filters on it, and a database rule such as Postgres row level security can act as a second lock in case code forgets. JSON: api/multi-tenant-isolation.json
- [Two-factor authentication (TOTP)](e/two-factor-auth/index.html): After the password, the user types a 6-digit code from an authenticator app. You store a secret per user, check codes with a small time window, and give recovery codes for when the phone is gone. JSON: api/two-factor-auth.json
- [Passkeys (WebAuthn)](e/passkeys/index.html): Sign-in with a key pair stored on the user's phone, laptop or password manager, unlocked with Face ID, a fingerprint or a PIN. Your server keeps only the public key, so there's no password to phish or leak. JSON: api/passkeys.json
- [Email verification](e/email-verification/index.html): Sending a one-time link or code to the address a user gives and marking it verified only when they use it. It proves they own the inbox before you send them anything important or let that address reset a password. JSON: api/email-verification.json
- [Team invite flow](e/team-invites/index.html): A way for a member to add someone by email. You create an invite with a random token, role and expiry, email a link, and on accept you check the signed-in person matches the invited address before adding them. JSON: api/team-invites.json
- [Support impersonation](e/impersonation/index.html): A controlled way for staff to see the app as a specific user, with a banner that shows it's happening, a time limit, an audit trail and blocks on dangerous actions like changing passwords or payments. JSON: api/impersonation.json

### Email and notifications

- [Email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)](e/email-authentication/index.html): Three DNS records that let inbox providers check that mail really comes from you. SPF lists which servers may send for your domain. DKIM signs each message with a key published in DNS. DMARC says what to do when those checks fail and where to send reports. JSON: api/email-authentication.json
- [Transactional vs bulk email](e/transactional-vs-bulk-email/index.html): Transactional email is one message to one person because of something they did: a sign-in link, a receipt, a reset. Bulk email is the same message to many people: newsletters, announcements. Send them through separate streams or providers so complaints about one don't hurt delivery of the other, and send from a background job, not inside the web request. JSON: api/transactional-vs-bulk-email.json
- [Unsubscribe and suppression list](e/unsubscribe-handling/index.html): A way for people to stop marketing email, honored quickly, plus a list of addresses you never mail again: unsubscribes, hard bounces and spam complaints. Gmail requires bulk senders to support one-click unsubscribe through the List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers (RFC 8058). JSON: api/unsubscribe-handling.json
- [Push notifications](e/push-notifications/index.html): Messages that appear on a device even when your app isn't open. On the web, a service worker receives them through the browser's push service, signed with your VAPID keys. iPhones support web push only for sites added to the home screen (iOS 16.4 and later). Native apps use APNs (Apple) and FCM (Google). JSON: api/push-notifications.json
- [Inbound email parsing](e/inbound-email/index.html): Letting your app receive email. A provider accepts mail for an address or domain you own, turns each message into JSON (sender, subject, text, attachments) and posts it to a webhook in your app. JSON: api/inbound-email.json
- [SMS text messages](e/sms-messages/index.html): Sending text messages through a provider's API. The code is easy. The work is registration (in the US, 10DLC brand and campaign approval for business texting), consent, STOP handling, cost per message, and fraud on verification codes. JSON: api/sms-messages.json
- [Notification preferences and inbox](e/notification-preferences/index.html): A per-user record of which notification types they want on which channel (email, push, in-app), and an in-app list of recent notifications with read state. Every send checks the preferences first. JSON: api/notification-preferences.json

### Files and uploads

- [Signed download link](e/signed-download-links/index.html): A URL with an expiry time and a signature built in. Anyone with the link can download until it expires, and changing any part of it breaks the signature. The files stay private by default. JSON: api/signed-download-links.json
- [Direct-to-storage uploads](e/direct-uploads/index.html): Your server hands the browser a short-lived signed URL, and the browser sends the file straight to object storage. Your app never holds the bytes, so big files don't tie up workers or hit request size limits. Your server still decides who can upload, what key the file gets and how big it can be. JSON: api/direct-uploads.json
- [Image resizing and thumbnails](e/image-resizing/index.html): Making smaller copies of uploaded images at the sizes your pages show, in modern formats, so pages load fast. Do it once when the image arrives, or on request through an image service that caches the result. JSON: api/image-resizing.json
- [Upload validation and scanning](e/upload-validation-scanning/index.html): Checking every uploaded file on the server before you keep it: its real type from its bytes, its size, and its contents where that matters. Then store it under a name you choose and serve it so the browser can't run it as a page. JSON: api/upload-validation-scanning.json
- [CSV import](e/csv-import/index.html): Taking a user's spreadsheet and turning rows into records. The safe shape is upload, map columns, preview with row-level errors, then commit all at once, with a row limit and the same validation as your forms. JSON: api/csv-import.json
- [PDF generation](e/pdf-generation/index.html): Turning your data into a PDF file users can download, print or send. Either render HTML with a headless browser or a print-CSS engine, or draw the document directly with a PDF library. Big documents go to a background job. JSON: api/pdf-generation.json

### Data and databases

- [Backups with a tested restore](e/backups-tested-restore/index.html): A backup only counts once you have restored it. Back up the database and uploaded files on a schedule, copy them off the server, and regularly restore into a throwaway database to prove they work. JSON: api/backups-tested-restore.json
- [Safe database migrations](e/database-migrations/index.html): Changing the database schema in small steps that the old and new versions of your code can both live with, checked in CI and run as a release step. Renames and drops happen in two releases: add the new shape, move the code and data, then remove the old shape. JSON: api/database-migrations.json
- [Database connection pooling](e/connection-pooling/index.html): Reusing a small set of open database connections instead of opening a new one for each request. Postgres handles a limited number of connections, and serverless functions can open hundreds at once, so a pooler sits in between and shares a few real connections. JSON: api/connection-pooling.json
- [Soft delete and restore](e/soft-delete/index.html): Marking a record as deleted instead of removing it, so it disappears from the app but can be restored. A purge job removes it for real after a set time, which also matters when someone asks you to erase their data. JSON: api/soft-delete.json
- [Audit log](e/audit-log/index.html): An append-only record of important actions: who did what to which record, when, and from where, with the values before and after. It answers support questions and security reviews, and some customers require it. JSON: api/audit-log.json
- [Transactions and race conditions](e/transactions-race-conditions/index.html): Making a group of database changes all happen or none happen, and making sure two requests running at the same moment can't both pass a check that only one should pass. Check-then-write code is the usual bug: both requests read the old value before either writes. JSON: api/transactions-race-conditions.json
- [Pagination](e/pagination/index.html): Returning a list a page at a time instead of all at once. Offset paging (page 3 of 20) is simple and fine for small lists. Cursor paging (give me the 25 after this one) stays fast on big tables and doesn't skip or repeat items when rows are added while someone scrolls. JSON: api/pagination.json
- [Storing money amounts](e/money-amounts/index.html): Keeping money exact. Store amounts as whole minor units (cents) in an integer column, or as a fixed DECIMAL, always next to a currency code. Never use floating point for money, and round once, at a defined step. JSON: api/money-amounts.json

### APIs and integrations

- [Outgoing webhooks](e/outbound-webhooks/index.html): Your app calls a URL your user gave you each time an event happens, like order.paid or report.ready. Done right, every delivery is signed, saved, retried with backoff and visible in a log, so a customer's slow server can't slow you down. JSON: api/outbound-webhooks.json
- [API keys for your own API](e/api-keys/index.html): Long random secrets your users create so their scripts can call your API without a password. You show the key once, store only a hash of it, and let users name, scope and revoke each one. JSON: api/api-keys.json
- [API versioning plan](e/api-versioning/index.html): A written rule for how your API changes over time: what counts as breaking, how a new version is chosen by callers, and how long old versions keep working. Adding fields is usually safe. Removing or renaming them is not. JSON: api/api-versioning.json
- [Idempotency keys for your API](e/idempotency-keys/index.html): The caller sends a unique key with each create request. Your API saves the key with the result, and if the same key comes back it returns the saved result instead of doing the work again. Retrying after a timeout becomes safe. JSON: api/idempotency-keys.json
- [API docs from an OpenAPI spec](e/api-docs-openapi/index.html): One machine-readable file that describes every endpoint, field and error of your API. Reference pages, client libraries and contract tests are generated from it, so the docs can't drift far from the code. JSON: api/api-docs-openapi.json
- [Timeouts and circuit breakers](e/timeouts-circuit-breakers/index.html): A timeout puts a limit on how long you wait for another service. A circuit breaker watches for repeated failures and, once there are too many, stops calling that service for a while and fails right away. Together they keep one slow dependency from tying up your whole app or running up a bill. JSON: api/timeouts-circuit-breakers.json

### Security and abuse

- [Rate limiting](e/rate-limiting/index.html): Count requests per key (IP address, user or API key) in a time window and refuse with 429 once the count passes the limit. JSON: api/rate-limiting.json
- [Ownership checks (IDOR)](e/ownership-checks/index.html): Checking on every request that the logged-in user is allowed to touch the exact record they asked for. The usual bug: the code loads a record by id and never checks who owns it. Hard-to-guess ids help but don't replace the check. JSON: api/ownership-checks.json
- [Input validation](e/input-validation/index.html): Checking every piece of incoming data on the server against what you expect: type, length, format and allowed values. Anything else is rejected before your code uses it. Browser checks only help the user. Anyone can skip them. JSON: api/input-validation.json
- [CORS settings](e/cors/index.html): Headers your API sends to tell browsers which other websites may read its responses. CORS only loosens the browser's same-origin rule. It doesn't stop scripts, servers or curl from calling your API, so it never replaces authentication. JSON: api/cors.json
- [CSRF protection](e/csrf/index.html): Stopping other websites from making a logged-in user's browser send state-changing requests to your app. It matters when login lives in cookies, because the browser attaches them automatically. APIs that only accept a token in the Authorization header aren't exposed in the same way. JSON: api/csrf.json
- [Secrets management](e/secrets-management/index.html): Keeping API keys, passwords and signing keys out of your code, your git history and the browser. They live in your host's secret settings or a secrets manager, the app reads them at startup, and you know how to replace each one quickly if it leaks. JSON: api/secrets-management.json
- [SSRF protection](e/ssrf-protection/index.html): Guarding any feature where your server fetches a URL that a user supplied. Without it, someone can point your server at internal addresses, like a cloud metadata endpoint or an admin panel on localhost, and read the response through your app. JSON: api/ssrf-protection.json
- [Bot and spam protection](e/bot-protection/index.html): Stopping automated traffic on forms that cost you money or reputation: signup, login, contact, checkout and anything that sends email or calls an AI. Layers work best: a hidden honeypot field, a challenge like Turnstile checked on the server, and rate limits behind both. JSON: api/bot-protection.json
- [Security headers (CSP, HSTS)](e/security-headers/index.html): Response headers that tell the browser how strict to be with your pages: HTTPS only (HSTS), who may frame you, which scripts and connections are allowed (CSP), and what features like the camera or location are off. JSON: api/security-headers.json
- [Dependency updates and audits](e/dependency-updates/index.html): A routine for keeping third-party packages current and checked against known vulnerabilities: pinned versions in a lockfile, automatic update pull requests, and an audit step that fails the build on serious issues. JSON: api/dependency-updates.json
- [Sanitizing user HTML and markdown (XSS)](e/html-sanitizing/index.html): Making sure text users write can't run as code in other people's browsers. Escape by default everywhere, and when you must allow formatting, run the HTML through an allowlist sanitizer on the server before saving or showing it. JSON: api/html-sanitizing.json
- [Field-level encryption](e/field-encryption/index.html): Encrypting chosen columns in your app before they reach the database, with a key the database never sees. A stolen backup or database dump then shows ciphertext for those fields. It needs a plan for keys, rotation and search. JSON: api/field-encryption.json

### Deploys, uptime and monitoring

- [Feature flag](e/feature-flags/index.html): A named on and off switch the code checks at runtime. You deploy with the feature off, turn it on for everyone, some users or just yourself, and turn it off fast if it breaks. JSON: api/feature-flags.json
- [Health checks and safe deploys](e/health-checks/index.html): Small URLs your platform calls to ask two things: is the process alive (liveness), and can it serve traffic right now, with the database, cache and migrations in order (readiness). Deploy tools wait for readiness before sending traffic to a new version and keep the old one if it never gets there. JSON: api/health-checks.json
- [Error tracking](e/error-tracking/index.html): A service that catches unhandled errors in your server and browser code, groups repeats together, and alerts you with the stack trace. You learn about bugs before users report them. It also collects whatever data you let it, so set it up to avoid personal data. JSON: api/error-tracking.json
- [Structured logging](e/structured-logging/index.html): Writing logs as data, one JSON object per event with fields like event name, user id, request id and duration, instead of free text. Then you can search and count them, and follow one request through every service it touched. JSON: api/structured-logging.json
- [Uptime monitoring](e/uptime-monitoring/index.html): An outside service that checks your site every minute or so and alerts you when it fails. Heartbeat checks do the reverse for jobs: the job pings the monitor when it finishes, and you're alerted when the ping doesn't arrive. JSON: api/uptime-monitoring.json
- [Staging environment](e/staging-environment/index.html): A second copy of your app that runs the same code and setup as production but with its own database, keys and test-mode payments. You deploy there first, click through the change, and then promote the same build to production. JSON: api/staging-environment.json
- [Rollback plan](e/rollback/index.html): A tested way to put the last working version back in minutes. Keep the previous build around, know which database changes it can live with, and practice the switch before you need it. JSON: api/rollback.json
- [Status page](e/status-page/index.html): A public page, hosted away from your app, that shows whether each part of your service is working and lists incidents and planned maintenance with updates. It answers "is it just me?" without a support email. JSON: api/status-page.json
- [CI checks on every push](e/ci-pipeline/index.html): An automatic run of your tests, linters, type checks and build on every push or pull request. A red result blocks the merge or deploy, so a change that breaks something is caught in minutes instead of by users. JSON: api/ci-pipeline.json
- [Custom domains for customers](e/customer-custom-domains/index.html): Letting each customer serve their part of your app from their own domain, like docs.theircompany.com. They add a DNS record, you verify it, issue an HTTPS certificate automatically, and route requests by hostname to the right account. JSON: api/customer-custom-domains.json

### AI features

- [Streaming AI responses](e/streaming-ai-responses/index.html): Sending the model's answer to the browser piece by piece as it's generated, usually over server-sent events, so people see text within a second instead of waiting for the whole reply. Your server sits in the middle, keeps the API key private, and saves the finished answer. JSON: api/streaming-ai-responses.json
- [LLM retries, timeouts and fallbacks](e/llm-retries-fallbacks/index.html): Treating the model API like any network service that will sometimes be slow or fail. Set timeouts, retry only the errors worth retrying with backoff, and decide what users see when it's still failing: a cheaper model, a simpler non-AI result, or a clear message. JSON: api/llm-retries-fallbacks.json
- [AI spend caps and token budgets](e/token-budget/index.html): Putting a ceiling on AI spending at every level: maximum tokens per request, an allowance per user or plan, and an alert or hard stop for the whole account. Record usage for each call so you know which features and users cost what. JSON: api/token-budget.json
- [Prompt injection defenses](e/prompt-injection/index.html): Limiting the damage when text the model reads, from a user or from a document, email or web page, contains instructions. No prompt wording fully stops this, so the real defenses are what the model is allowed to do: least-privilege tools, confirmation for risky actions, and treating its output as untrusted. JSON: api/prompt-injection.json
- [Structured output from LLMs](e/structured-output/index.html): Getting the model to return data in a fixed shape your code can rely on. Use the provider's schema feature where it exists, then validate the result anyway and decide what happens when it doesn't fit: retry once, fall back, or show an error. JSON: api/structured-output.json
- [LLM evals](e/llm-evals/index.html): A saved set of real inputs with what a good answer must contain or avoid, run every time you change a prompt, model or setting. It turns 'seems fine' into a score you can compare, so upgrades don't quietly break cases that used to work. JSON: api/llm-evals.json
- [Prompt caching](e/prompt-caching/index.html): A provider feature that reuses the processed start of a prompt when the next request begins with exactly the same text. Repeated instructions, documents and chat history cost less and return faster. Put the parts that never change first and the changing parts last. JSON: api/prompt-caching.json
- [Content moderation](e/content-moderation/index.html): Checking what users post or generate for abuse, and having a way for people to report it and for you to act. Combine an automatic classifier, user reports, a review queue and clear actions like hide, warn and ban. JSON: api/content-moderation.json
- [LLM tool calling](e/tool-calling/index.html): Giving the model a list of functions it may ask you to run, each with a name, description and input schema. Your code checks permissions, runs the function, and sends back the result. The model never touches your systems directly. JSON: api/tool-calling.json
- [AI chat history storage](e/chat-history/index.html): Tables for conversations and messages, plus a rule for how much history goes back to the model each turn. Older turns get trimmed or summarized so long chats stay inside the context window and the cost stays sane. JSON: api/chat-history.json

### Performance and caching

- [Caching and invalidation](e/caching-invalidation/index.html): Keeping the result of slow or costly work for a while so the next request can reuse it. The hard parts are the key (it must include everything the result depends on, including the user) and knowing when the saved copy is out of date. JSON: api/caching-invalidation.json
- [CDN and static asset caching](e/cdn/index.html): Serving files that are the same for everyone, like CSS, JavaScript, fonts and images, from servers close to the user, with file names that change when the content changes. Then browsers can cache them for a year, and a deploy still shows the new version at once. JSON: api/cdn.json
- [Database indexes](e/database-indexes/index.html): Lookup structures that let the database find rows without reading the whole table. Most slow pages in young apps come from a missing index on the columns a query filters and sorts by, or from N+1 queries that run one query per row. JSON: api/database-indexes.json
- [Load testing](e/load-testing/index.html): Sending realistic fake traffic at a copy of your app to find where it slows down or breaks: requests per second, response times at the 95th percentile, errors, and which part (database, CPU, an outside API) gives out first. JSON: api/load-testing.json
- [N+1 query fixes](e/n-plus-one-queries/index.html): A common ORM slowdown: one query loads a list, then one more query runs for each item to fetch related data. Load the related data in one or two queries up front (eager loading or batching) instead. JSON: api/n-plus-one-queries.json
- [Debounce and throttle](e/debouncing/index.html): Two ways to stop a fast stream of events from doing work every time. Debounce waits until the user pauses, then runs once, which suits search boxes and autosave. Throttle runs at most once every so often, which suits scroll, resize and drag handlers. JSON: api/debouncing.json

### Search

- [Full-text search](e/full-text-search/index.html): Search that matches words, not exact strings: it handles plurals and word forms, ranks the best matches first, and stays fast as data grows. Postgres can do this well before you need a separate search engine. JSON: api/full-text-search.json
- [Semantic search and RAG](e/semantic-search/index.html): Turning text into embeddings (lists of numbers that capture meaning) so you can find passages similar to a question even when the words differ. RAG feeds the best passages to a model so it answers from your content instead of guessing. JSON: api/semantic-search.json
- [Keeping a search index in sync](e/search-index-sync/index.html): The jobs that copy changes from your database into a separate search engine. Every create, update and delete queues an index update, a full rebuild can run into a fresh index and swap over, and a check catches drift. JSON: api/search-index-sync.json

### Common app features

- [Translations and localization (i18n)](e/i18n/index.html): Pulling every user-facing string out of the code into translation files, picking a language per user, and formatting dates, numbers, currencies and plurals with the locale's rules. Done early, it's cheap. Done late, it means touching every screen. JSON: api/i18n.json
- [Calendar feeds and invites (ICS)](e/calendar-feeds/index.html): Publishing events in the iCalendar format so Google, Apple and Outlook calendars can show them. A one-off .ics file adds a single event. A private subscription URL lets the user's calendar refresh your events on its own schedule. JSON: api/calendar-feeds.json
- [Location and distance search](e/geolocation/index.html): Storing latitude and longitude for things, turning addresses into coordinates (geocoding), and querying by distance with a spatial index. The user's own location comes from the browser with permission, or from a typed address or postcode. JSON: api/geolocation.json
- [Live updates (WebSockets, SSE or polling)](e/realtime-updates/index.html): Getting changes to the browser as they happen. Polling asks every few seconds. Server-sent events stream one way from server to browser. WebSockets go both ways. Pick the simplest one that meets the delay users will notice. JSON: api/realtime-updates.json
- [Internal admin panel](e/admin-panel/index.html): A private part of your app for you and your staff to find users, see their records, and fix common problems with buttons instead of raw SQL. Every action checks staff roles and lands in the audit log. JSON: api/admin-panel.json
- [Optimistic updates](e/optimistic-updates/index.html): Showing the result of an action on screen the moment the user clicks, then sending it to the server in the background. If the server says no, you put the old value back and tell the user. It makes small actions like likes, checkboxes and reordering feel instant. JSON: api/optimistic-updates.json
- [Autosave and drafts](e/autosave-drafts/index.html): Saving what a user is writing every few seconds without them pressing Save, usually as a draft that only becomes the real record when they finish. A refresh, crash or dead battery then costs them a few seconds of typing, not the whole thing. JSON: api/autosave-drafts.json

### Analytics and privacy

- [Cookie consent and privacy-friendly analytics](e/cookie-consent/index.html): Asking before you set non-essential cookies or load trackers, where the law requires it, and not loading them until people agree. Many apps avoid most of the problem by using cookieless, privacy-focused analytics and keeping ad pixels off logged-in pages. JSON: api/cookie-consent.json
- [Data export and account deletion](e/data-export-deletion/index.html): Self-serve tools for users to download their data in a usable format and to delete their account. Deleting means removing their records and files, cancelling their billing, and telling them what's kept and why, like backups that expire or legal records. JSON: api/data-export-deletion.json
- [Data retention and cleanup](e/data-retention/index.html): A written list of what data you keep, for how long and why, plus scheduled jobs that delete or anonymize it when time is up. It covers logs, backups, temporary files, expired tokens and closed accounts. JSON: api/data-retention.json
- [Product analytics events](e/product-analytics/index.html): Sending a small named event when a user does something that matters, like signing up, finishing setup or upgrading, so you can count each step and see where people stop. Page views tell you traffic. Events tell you whether the product is working. JSON: api/product-analytics.json

## Data

- [entries.json](entries.json): all entries with prompts and checks
